AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: Sport climbers strain passive and active anatomical structures of their hands and fingers to the maximum during training or competition. This study was designed to investigate bone marrow edema (BME) in rock climbing athletes.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Systematic detection, treatment, and follow-up investigation of rock climbing athletes with BME of the hand.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Primary-level orthopedic surgery and sports medicine division of a large academic medical center.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: Thirty-one high-level climbers with diffuse pain in the hand and wrist joint caused by rock climbing were included in this study.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTIONS
AbstractText.content: The therapy consisted of consequent stress reduction and a break from sports.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Reduction of BME shown through magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and regaining of preinjury climbing levels (Union Internationale des Associations d' Alpinisme metric scale).

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: In 28 patients, MRI revealed osseous edema because of overload at the respective area of interest, mainly in the distal radius, the distal ulna, or the carpal bones, which could not be otherwise diagnosed as inflammations, tumors, or injuries. We classified these edemas and fractures of the hamate because of overload. The edema was a stress reaction to highly intensive training and climbing with presumably high traction to the wrist area. The control MRIs demonstrated that even with a consequent stress reduction, the edemas required 3 to 4 months to disappear completely.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Climbers with nonspecific, diffuse pain in the wrist and/or the fingers should be examined with MRI to detect or exclude the diagnosis of a BME.
